t: LeetCode 405 — Convert a Number to Hexadecimal
o: We must render any 32-bit signed integer as lowercase hexadecimal without built-in conversion helpers. Positive numbers are straightforward positional notation in base 16; the twist is that negative numbers must be shown as their 32-bit two's complement pattern, e.g. -1 becomes "ffffffff" because all 32 bits are set. For Example 1, num = 26: 26 = 1·16 + 10, digit 10 maps to 'a', so the answer is "1a". For Example 2, num = -1: its two's complement bit pattern is 0xFFFFFFFF, which reads directly as "ffffffff". Since the input always fits in 32 bits, the output has at most 8 hex characters, which means any reasonable loop runs at most 8 times — every correct approach is effectively O(1); the only real design decisions are how to obtain the unsigned view of a negative number and whether to divide or mask-and-shift.
k: A negative 32-bit integer's two's complement is just its value interpreted as unsigned, i.e. add 2^32 (or cast to unsigned / use logical shift) — no special-case logic per sign is needed.
Each hex digit is exactly one nibble: extract with num & 0xF and advance with a 4-bit logical right shift, avoiding division entirely.
The result never exceeds 8 characters, and num = 0 must be special-cased to return "0" instead of an empty string.

a.n: Approach 1: Normalize then repeated division (brute force)
a.i: If num is negative, convert it to the equivalent positive unsigned value by adding 2^32 — this is precisely what two's complement represents. Then repeatedly take num mod 16 to get the next least-significant hex digit and integer-divide by 16, collecting digits in reverse order. This mirrors how you'd convert bases by hand and needs no bit tricks.
s: If num < 0, replace num with num + 2^32.
Map remainders 0-15 to characters via the lookup string "0123456789abcdef".
While num > 0, append digits[num % 16], then set num = floor(num / 16).
Reverse the collected digits and return them.
a.t: O(1) time — at most 8 iterations since a 32-bit value has at most 8 hex digits.
a.sp: O(1) space — the result string is bounded by 8 characters.

a.n: Approach 2: Bit masking with logical shifts (optimal)
a.i: Hexadecimal is base 16 = 2^4, so each hex digit corresponds to exactly 4 bits. Masking the low 4 bits with num & 0xF yields the current digit, and a *logical* (unsigned) right shift by 4 discards those bits without sign-extension. Using the logical shift means negative numbers automatically expose their two's complement bit pattern, so no explicit 2^32 adjustment is required. Loop until the value becomes 0 (or 8 digits are produced).
s: While num != 0 and fewer than 8 digits have been produced:
Append digits[num & 15] to the front (or append and reverse at the end).
Set num = num >>> 4 (logical right shift; in Python mask first with 0xFFFFFFFF, in C++ operate on an unsigned int).
a.t: O(1) time — each iteration consumes 4 bits of a fixed 32-bit word, so at most 8 iterations.
a.sp: O(1) space — only the ≤ 8-character output buffer.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 to show you understand two's complement as 'value + 2^32', then upgrade to the mask-and-shift version, explicitly calling out that the shift must be *logical* (>>> in Java/JS, unsigned int in C++, pre-masking in Python). Common pitfalls: (1) using arithmetic >> on a negative int in C++/Java causes an infinite loop because sign-extension keeps the value negative; (2) forgetting num = 0, which would yield an empty string instead of "0"; (3) emitting leading zeros — only extract digits while the value is nonzero; (4) off-by-one on the 8-digit cap for negative inputs like Integer.MIN_VALUE. Likely follow-ups: generalize to any base 2–36 (same loop, bigger digit table, careful with the 2^32 offset), produce binary or octal strings, or do it without extra space beyond the output.
